topic: Balanced forces; net force; static & dynamic equilibrium; inertia
source_citation: OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.2 'Newton's First Law of Motion: Inertia' (CC-BY 4.0); NGSS MS-PS2-1 DCI PS2.A; Utah SEEd Std 7.1.1; OpenStax University Physics Vol 1 §5.2
ground_truth_fact_1: Newton's First Law: A body at rest remains at rest — or if in motion remains in motion at constant velocity — unless acted on by a net external force. (OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.2)
ground_truth_fact_2: When ΣF = 0 the object has zero acceleration. It is in mechanical equilibrium — either static (at rest) or dynamic (constant velocity). (OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.2)
ground_truth_fact_3: Balanced forces ≠ 'no forces.' Balanced means the vector sum of all forces equals zero while individual forces still act on the object. (NGSS PS2.A)
ground_truth_fact_4: Inertia is the tendency of an object to resist changes in its state of motion. Mass is the quantitative measure of inertia. (OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.2)
ground_truth_fact_5: The greater the mass of an object the greater the force needed to achieve the same change in motion. (NGSS PS2.A; OpenStax §4.2)
ground_truth_fact_6: An object moving at constant speed in a straight line has balanced forces acting on it — the same equilibrium condition as a stationary object. (OpenStax §4.2)
ground_truth_fact_7: For a box sliding at constant velocity with applied force +50 N the friction force must be −50 N so ΣF = 0. (OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.2 worked example)
narrative_scenario: A 50 kg inspection robot is tethered between two magnetic winches on a frictionless orbital rail. Both winches are pulling — yet the robot glides at a rock-steady 2 m/s without speeding up or slowing down. Ground control says the forces are 'balanced.' But if forces are pulling on it from both sides how can it keep moving at all?
narrative_mission_objective: Adjust the left and right force sliders until the robot's acceleration reads exactly 0 m/s² — then explain why a net force of zero does NOT mean the robot must stop.
physics_extra_constants: F_net = F_left − F_right; a = F_net / m; ΣF = 0 ↔ equilibrium
placement_q1_text: A box slides at constant speed across a frictionless surface. What is the net force acting on it?
placement_q1_options: Zero net force|A force in the direction of motion|A force opposing the motion|Gravity only
placement_q2_text: Two teams pull a rope with equal force (50 N each) in opposite directions. Describe what happens to the rope and explain why — using Newton's First Law.
placement_q2_sample_answer: The rope does not accelerate because the forces are balanced: net force = 50 N − 50 N = 0 N. With zero net force there is zero acceleration (Newton's First Law). The rope either stays still or keeps moving at constant velocity.
valerie_target_misconception: Students confuse 'balanced forces' with 'no forces at all.' They believe an object must be stationary for forces to be balanced — missing that constant-velocity motion also means ΣF = 0.
valerie_socratic_clue_1: The robot is moving but not accelerating. If no net force is needed to KEEP an object moving — what IS a net force needed for?
valerie_socratic_clue_2: Look at the acceleration readout. It reads 0 m/s². Now look at the velocity readout — is the robot stopped or still moving? What does that tell you?
valerie_socratic_clue_3: You set left force = right force and got a = 0. Try making them unequal. What happens to the velocity now? What changed?
valerie_mastery_criteria: Student articulates that balanced forces (ΣF = 0) produce zero acceleration — meaning NO CHANGE in velocity — and that an object can be moving at constant velocity with zero net force. Student must distinguish 'balanced forces' from 'no forces.'

topic: Non-contact magnetic forces; magnetic fields; force–distance relationship; field mapping
source_citation: NGSS MS-PS2-5 DCI PS2.B (CC-BY); NGSS MS-PS2-3 DCI PS2.B; OpenStax College Physics 2e §22.4 (CC-BY 4.0); Utah SEEd Std 7.1.4; Wikipedia 'Magnetic Dipole' (CC-BY-SA)
ground_truth_fact_1: Magnetic forces are non-contact forces — they act between objects that are not physically touching through invisible fields that extend through space. (NGSS PS2.B)
ground_truth_fact_2: Forces that act at a distance (electric magnetic gravitational) can be explained by fields that extend through space and can be mapped by their effect on a test object. (NGSS MS-PS2-5 DCI PS2.B)
ground_truth_fact_3: Electric and magnetic forces can be attractive or repulsive and their sizes depend on the magnitudes of the charges/currents/magnetic strengths and on the distances between the interacting objects. (NGSS PS2.B via MS-PS2-3)
ground_truth_fact_4: The magnetic field strength of a bar magnet (dipole) decreases approximately as 1/r³ (inverse-cube law) because magnetic poles always exist in north-south pairs — no monopoles. (Wikipedia 'Magnetic Dipole'; Vaia Physics Ch 11)
ground_truth_fact_5: The force between two magnetic dipoles decreases approximately as 1/r⁴ along their common axis. Doubling the distance reduces the force to roughly 1/16 of the original. (NASA GSFC Dipole Properties)
ground_truth_fact_6: Magnetic fields can be visualized using iron filings or a compass — field lines form closed loops exiting the north pole and entering the south pole outside the magnet. (OpenStax College Physics 2e §22.4)
ground_truth_fact_7: At the middle-school level NGSS limits assessment to QUALITATIVE evidence for the existence of fields — no inverse-square or inverse-cube calculations required. (NGSS MS-PS2-5 Assessment Boundary)
ground_truth_fact_8: Magnetic force drops off far more steeply than gravitational or Coulomb force — a magnet that grips a paperclip at 1 cm may have no noticeable pull at 5 cm.
narrative_scenario: Two powerful neodymium magnets sit on a frictionless measurement rail in the school lab. When they are 1 cm apart the force sensor reads 8.0 N — strong enough to leap across the gap. A student slides one magnet to 2 cm apart and expects the force to halve. Instead the sensor plummets to roughly 1.0 N. Something about this force is far more dramatic than a simple linear drop-off.
narrative_mission_objective: Drag the movable magnet along the rail and record force readings at 5 different distances. Identify the mathematical pattern and predict the force at a distance you have NOT yet measured.
physics_target_equilibrium_condition: qualitative: force increases dramatically as distance approaches zero
physics_extra_constants: F_dipole ∝ 1/r⁴ (axial); B_dipole ∝ μ₀·m/(4π·r³); at MS level: closer = much stronger
placement_q1_text: If you move two magnets from 1 cm apart to 2 cm apart what happens to the magnetic force between them?
placement_q1_options: It roughly halves|It stays the same|It drops to about one-eighth|It drops to about one-quarter
placement_q2_text: A student moves two bar magnets from 2 cm apart to 6 cm apart (tripling the distance). Describe and explain the change in force.
placement_q2_sample_answer: The force drops dramatically — far more than by a factor of 3. For magnetic dipoles the field falls as 1/r³ so tripling the distance reduces the field to about 1/27 of the original. The force between dipoles drops even faster (≈ 1/r⁴). Students should recognize the nonlinear rapid decrease.
valerie_target_misconception: Students assume magnetic force decreases linearly with distance — 'twice as far = half the force.' They do not recognize the rapid nonlinear drop-off and drastically underestimate how quickly force weakens.
valerie_socratic_clue_1: You expected the force to halve when you doubled the distance. Look at the actual reading — is it half? More? Less? By how much?
valerie_socratic_clue_2: Compare your 1 cm reading to your 2 cm reading. Now compare your 2 cm reading to your 4 cm reading. Is the RATIO the same? What does that tell you about the pattern?
valerie_socratic_clue_3: If the force dropped by a factor of 8 when you doubled the distance from 1 cm to 2 cm — predict what happens at 3 cm. Now measure it. Were you close?
valerie_mastery_criteria: Student explains that magnetic force decreases nonlinearly with distance — it drops off much faster than a simple halving. Student provides data evidence showing the rapid decay pattern and connects it to the concept of a field that weakens with distance.

topic: Net force; mass; acceleration; F = ma; direct & inverse proportionality; kinematics
source_citation: OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.3 'Newton's Second Law of Motion' (CC-BY 4.0); OpenStax University Physics Vol 1 §5.3 (CC-BY 4.0); NGSS MS-PS2-2 DCI PS2.A; Utah SEEd Std 7.1.1
ground_truth_fact_1: Newton's Second Law: The acceleration of a system is directly proportional to and in the same direction as the net external force acting on the system and inversely proportional to its mass. a = F_net / m. (OpenStax College Physics 2e §4.3)
ground_truth_fact_2: Acceleration is directly proportional to net force: doubling the force doubles the acceleration when mass is held constant. (OpenStax §4.3)
ground_truth_fact_3: Acceleration is inversely proportional to mass: doubling the mass halves the acceleration when force is held constant. (OpenStax §4.3)
ground_truth_fact_4: The SI unit of force is the newton: 1 N = 1 kg·m/s². A newton is the force needed to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s². (OpenStax §4.3)
ground_truth_fact_5: When F_net = 0 then a = 0. Newton's First Law is a special case of the Second Law. (OpenStax University Physics Vol 1 §5.3)
ground_truth_fact_6: The acceleration vector always points in the same direction as the net force vector. (OpenStax University Physics Vol 1 §5.3)
ground_truth_fact_7: Kinematics under constant acceleration: v = v₀ + a·t; x = x₀ + v₀·t + ½·a·t². These connect force to observable motion. (OpenStax §4.3)
ground_truth_fact_8: NGSS MS-PS2-2 emphasizes qualitative comparisons of force mass and changes in motion — calculations limited to one dimension; no trigonometry required. (NGSS Assessment Boundary)
narrative_scenario: A rocket sled on a frictionless test track carries different cargo loads. Engineers fire the same 100 N thruster but get wildly different accelerations depending on how much cargo is loaded. With 10 kg of cargo the sled rockets forward at 10 m/s². With 50 kg it barely crawls at 2 m/s². The chief engineer asks: is there a single equation that predicts the acceleration for ANY combination of force and mass?
narrative_mission_objective: Independently adjust thrust force (10–200 N) and sled mass (5–100 kg). Collect at least 4 data points showing BOTH the force–acceleration AND mass–acceleration relationships. Build an evidence-based F = ma graph to complete the mission.
physics_extra_constants: a = F_net / m; F_net = m·a; 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²; v = v₀ + a·t; x = x₀ + v₀·t + ½·a·t²
placement_q1_text: A 10 kg cart is pushed with 30 N of net force. What is its acceleration?
placement_q2_text: If you keep the force the same but triple the mass of the sled what do you predict will happen to the acceleration? Use F = ma to justify your answer.
placement_q2_sample_answer: Acceleration will be one-third of the original. Since a = F/m tripling m while holding F constant divides a by 3. Example: if F = 30 N and m goes from 10 kg to 30 kg then a drops from 3 m/s² to 1 m/s².
valerie_target_misconception: Students memorize F = ma as a formula but don't grasp it as a causal relationship. They fail to predict that doubling mass halves acceleration (constant force) or that doubling force doubles acceleration (constant mass).
valerie_socratic_clue_1: You just doubled the force but the acceleration didn't seem to change much. Check your mass slider — did you accidentally change the mass too? What happens if you reset mass and ONLY change force?
valerie_socratic_clue_2: Compare Run 1 (low mass high force) to Run 2 (high mass same force). Which sled accelerated more? By what factor? Does that match what a = F/m predicts?
valerie_socratic_clue_3: Now hold mass constant and double the force. What happened to the acceleration? Is the relationship between force and acceleration a straight line or a curve?
valerie_mastery_criteria: Student demonstrates BOTH relationships: (1) acceleration doubles when force doubles at constant mass and (2) acceleration halves when mass doubles at constant force. Student connects observed data to a = F/m as a causal explanation — not just a memorized formula.
